name: Lateral (fibular) collateral ligament
description: Cord-like extracapsular ligament from just proximal and posterior to the lateral femoral epicondyle to the lateral fibular head, inserting between the biceps arms (the 'conjoined tendon' V). Low signal, about 3–6 mm thick, usually spread over 2–3 posterior coronal slices.
variants_pitfalls: Intermediate signal at the femoral attachment is normal (about 79% of knees); call a sprain only with periligamentous edema, thickening or fiber discontinuity.
Signal change and thickening are common in stable knees (a third each in one series, more with varus), so mild change alone does not mean prior injury.
Fluid around intact fibers at the fibular end is the fibular collateral–biceps bursa, not a tear. Separate slips with fat between them are normal; a true single conjoined insertion is rare.

In multiligament injuries it most often fails at the fibula (65%), where the biceps can mask it: check the fibular head and the common fibular nerve. Isolated LCL tears are rare; look at the popliteus, popliteofibular ligament and cruciates.
